p01.text: On March 4 the Israeli military announced that an F-35I Adir had shot down an Iranian Yak-130 over Tehran, the first time a stealth fighter had downed a manned military aircraft in combat. The same day, off Galle, Sri Lanka, a U.S. Navy submarine sank the Iranian frigate Dena on its way home from a naval review in India. Eighty-seven sailors died. Thirty-two were rescued.

p02.text: Israeli ground forces crossed into Lebanon and fought Hezbollah on the ground for the first time. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on gas exports. At Bandar Abbas a Soleimani-class corvette went down. CENTCOM said it had destroyed 20 Iranian vessels and struck about 2,000 targets since the war began. The Revolutionary Guards claimed they had blown up ten merchant ships. The strait did not open.

p03.text: On March 5 the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford passed through the Suez Canal, heading for the Red Sea. The war’s center of gravity was shifting south and east. In Tehran the 12,000-seat Azadi Indoor Stadium was destroyed. An Iranian drone came down on the terminal at Nakhchivan airport in Azerbaijan, and Azerbaijan pulled out its diplomats. The war was spreading beyond the Gulf.

p04.text: On March 6 heavy airstrikes hit Mehrabad Airport and other targets across Tehran. The rights group HRANA counted 664 strikes in 28 provinces in that single day. Iran widened its attacks to Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and the UAE. That evening President Masoud Pezeshkian went on state television and apologized for the attacks on neighboring countries.

p05.text: On March 7 the Israeli military said it had destroyed 16 Quds Force aircraft at Mehrabad. The tanker Prima was hit by a drone near Hormuz, and Kuwait Petroleum declared force majeure. Pezeshkian ordered units in the field to stop firing at will. The attacks went on anyway. The same day the United States sent a third aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, to the Middle East.

p06.text: March 4, afternoon, a private villa in Islamabad. The air conditioner was broken. On one side of the table sat a man from Tehran. He had no title. Across from him, a senior official of Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry. No Americans. Officially this room did not exist. The man from Tehran spoke first. “Seventy-two hours. If the bombing stops, the people on our side who can speak can get into one room.”

p07.text: “In whose name do you bring this?” The man did not answer. The Supreme Leader was dead, and no successor had been named. The keys to the missiles were not in the president’s hands. “Washington will ask about Fordow.” “Fordow is not in what I brought.” The Pakistani memorized one number. Seventy-two. Three days for one country to breathe become one line on another country’s desk.

p08.text: Dr. Leila Shirazi checked the signal three times. Then three more. The first time she put it down to a measurement error. The second time, interference. The third time she could not deny it any longer. The Fordow signal was getting stronger. The gaps were shrinking. The amplitude was rising. A broken system gives off an irregular signal. This one had a rule. Something completely dead cannot make a rule.

p09.text: She stopped in the middle of the report. There was the sentence she had written seven months ago. The only intervention capable of changing the trajectory is kinetic intervention. It had happened once last year, and had been going on now for five days. If that was not enough, what came next? She did not write the next sentence. At 5:51 a.m. she filed the report. The world lived the same moment at different hours.

p10.text: The pilot’s call sign was Saba. A major in the Israeli Air Force, thirty-five, from Tel Aviv. Her fifth sortie in five days. The target was a military complex east of Tehran. Then something showed up on the radar. An Iranian Yak-130. It was no match for a stealth fighter. The symbol turned. Not away. She followed procedure. The missile left the rail.

p11.text: A few dozen seconds later the symbol was gone from the screen. The other pilot would never have seen her. Someone who went up to fight what he could not see. Someone who must have known he would not come back. Who ran down the runway anyway. The machine had reduced him to one symbol. She could not erase the person behind it. Her radio report was calm. What was in those seconds stayed out of it.

p12.text: March 5, morning. Capt. Marcus Webb was passing between deserts. A hundred-thousand-ton ship moved down the canal at walking pace. In the canal, even a carrier waits in line. War correspondent Sarah Callahan came up to the bridge. No camera in her hands. “I heard about the Dena. Eighty-seven.” “She was headed home.” “She was a warship of a country at war.” After a long while he added, “Both are true.”

p13.text: “I’m getting off. By helicopter, once we’re in the Red Sea. The desk wants me in Bahrain.” “Bahrain’s being hit.” “I know. That’s why I’m going.” There was nothing more to say. It was a silence that held more than words. She went down first. He stayed and watched the channel. Sinking ships does not open the sea. Then what does?

p14.text: Lt. Kim Junho had been sitting with the phone in his hand for twenty minutes. Nine times he tried to call. Nine times he stopped at the button. If he heard his mother cry, he would cry too. That was what he was afraid of. War Day 6. He made the call. His mother picked up before the second ring had finished. It was 3:15 in the morning in Seoul. Six nights she had been waiting.

p15.text: “Junho.” That one word was enough. “I’m alive.” His voice shook less than he expected. “I know. We’re watching the news. Your father too.” A short silence. Her voice dropped almost to a whisper. “Sleep well.” That was all. She asked nothing. That made it bigger. Some wars are fought with guns. Some are fought by picking up the phone.

p16.text: The sun was going down. Three columns of smoke stood in the western sky. Mehrabad Airport had been hit that day, the Azadi Indoor Stadium the day before. Soraya Tahir was on the roof of a friend’s boarding house. The internet had been dead for six days. The city had lost every way to pass news. What was left was the oldest way. The voice. Soraya sang an old spring song.

p17.text: At first she was alone. At the second line a window opened across the way. At the third, someone on the next roof joined in. Two Basij motorcycles turned into the alley. The young militiaman on the back looked up at the roofs, and did not reach for the rifle on his shoulder. The order was in the front seat. The hesitation was in the back. Spring is older than war.

p18.text: Professor Azad Moradi took out the notebook he had bought in 1973 once more. Four days ago he had filled its last page. But last night’s singing from the roofs was still in his ears. He turned the notebook over. The inside of the back cover was blank. Yesterday the president had come on television and apologized. But after the apology, missiles still flew at the Gulf. The hand that spoke and the hand that fired were not on the same body.

p19.text: On the inside of the back cover he wrote. Last night the students sang on the roofs. Men with guns passed beneath them and did not shoot. Fifty-three years ago I wrote: truth is uncomfortable. Today I write: freedom is uncomfortable too. But oppression hurts longer. The bombs did not teach that. The people who sing beneath the bombs are teaching it.

p20.text: March 7. The Fordow signal changed again. Its amplitude was twice what it had been when she first caught it. Leila wrote down three possibilities. Old equipment overloading. Cascades being added one by one. And the one she feared most: someone had ordered them to speed up. To know, inspectors had to get in. For that, talks had to start. For talks, the bombing had to stop. It did not stop.

p21.text: She wrote one more report. Its last sentence was different from the one seven months ago. Kinetic intervention alone is not enough. The next step is diplomatic intervention. The more data piled up, the less certain she was. She drank a glass of water. It was cold. At that moment in Seoul, Kang Yujin was looking at a map of ships at Hormuz. Dots that did not move. When would they move again?
